title: Farhan Akhtar Is Becoming R.D. Burman. The Music Rights Are Already Locked.
excerpt: Neeraj Pandey's biopic of Pancham Da has secured the rights to his legendary tracks, and Farhan is preparing to step into the skin of the man who gave Hindi cinema its most unforgettable melodies.
body:
There is a short list of names in Hindi film music that need no context. **R.D. Burman** — Pancham Da — sits at the very top of it. The man who gave us "Chura Liya Hai Tumne Jo Dil Ko," who turned "Dum Maro Dum" into a generational anthem, who made "Mehbooba Mehbooba" sound like a fever dream you didn't want to wake from. And now, more than three decades after his death, someone is finally bringing his story to the screen.

**Farhan Akhtar** is in advanced talks to play R.D. Burman in a biographical drama directed by **Neeraj Pandey**, according to an exclusive report from Pinkvilla. The project has been in quiet development for some time, with Pandey and his writing team working at pace on a screenplay that aims to capture the full arc of a man who transformed Indian film music and was, for a stretch of the 1970s and '80s, its undisputed heartbeat.

> "Farhan Akhtar is in talks to play the legendary composer and is extremely excited about the prospect of bringing Pancham Da's journey to the big screen. If all goes according to plan, he will undergo extensive preparation to get into the skin of the character." — Source to Pinkvilla

The casting makes a kind of poetic sense. Farhan already lives in the space between filmmaking and music — he's a singer, a guitarist, and, most importantly, an actor who has proven he can disappear into a real person's life and make you believe it. His **Milkha Singh** in *Bhaag Milkha Bhaag* remains one of the finest biopic performances in Indian cinema. His **Aziz Ali** in *Toofaan* showed physical transformation at an almost punishing level. Now he's being asked to inhabit a man who was not an athlete but an artist — someone whose genius lived in melody, rhythm, and the melancholy that ran beneath his most joyous compositions.

Here's what makes this project feel genuinely ambitious, not just another Bollywood biopic with a costume department and a wiki page: **the makers have secured the rights to R.D. Burman's classic tracks**. The music — the actual music — will be part of the storytelling. Music sittings have already begun to bring the best versions of the original songs into the film's framework. Imagine scenes scored not with recreations or "inspired by" arrangements but with the architecture of the originals themselves. "Tere Bina Zindagi Se" playing under the weight of the man who composed it. "Aaj Kal Paon Zameen Par" carrying its creator's signature through a scene about love or loss or both.

The collaboration with **Neeraj Pandey** adds a particular flavour. Pandey's best work — *A Wednesday*, *Special 26*, *MS Dhoni: The Untold Story* — has always been precise, tight, and deeply researched. He doesn't make messy films. He doesn't sentimentalize. His *MS Dhoni*, in fact, is the gold standard for how Bollywood can handle a living legend's story without turning it into hagiography. Bringing that same discipline to R.D. Burman — a figure whose personal life was as dramatic as his discography, whose marriage to **Asha Bhosle** was the stuff of Bollywood itself, and whose career experienced a painful decline in the late '80s before his tragically early death at 54 — could produce something extraordinary.

The film is being co-produced by **Kamal Jain**, the producer behind *MS Dhoni: The Untold Story* and *Manikarnika*, and the plan is to take it to the floors by the end of 2026.

For the Indian diaspora, R.D. Burman is not just a musician. He's the soundtrack that followed you out of India. His songs play at weddings in New Jersey and Diwali parties in London. Your parents hummed "Roop Tera Mastana" on long drives. Your Spotify Wrapped probably had at least one of his tracks buried in the algorithm. He is, in a way, the shared cultural inheritance of every NRI household that kept one foot in Bombay no matter where they planted the other.

The timing is also notable. This development comes as Farhan navigates the well-publicized fallout around *Don 3*, where creative differences with **Ranveer Singh** reportedly led to the actor's exit. Rather than chasing another franchise play, Farhan appears to be pivoting toward something more personal, more musical — the kind of project that reminds you why he got into this business in the first place.

No official announcement has been made, and the project remains in pre-production. But the pieces — the director, the actor, the rights to the music, the production timeline — are falling into place with the kind of quiet momentum that suggests this isn't a rumour. It's a film waiting to happen.

Pancham Da once said that good music doesn't need anyone's permission to survive. He was right. But a good film about good music? That takes someone willing to do it justice. Farhan and Pandey look like they understand the assignment.
